title: Telus pulls out of two government-backed AI data centres in Vancouver | BetaKit
html:
Telus has pulled out of two AI data centre projects in Vancouver that former CEO Darren Entwistle announced alongside federal AI minister Evan Solomon just six months ago.

The news: Daily Hive reported on Saturday that the Canadian telecommunications giant is no longer partnered with local real estate developer Westbank on the AI data centre projects. When reached for comment, Westbank confirmed to BetaKit that Telus is no longer a partner on the two Vancouver projects. It did say, however, that it’s proceeding with the projects as planned and that a new partnership will be announced in the coming months.

When reached for comment, Solomon’s office deferred to Telus about its decision, but said Canada remains committed to building secure, sovereign computing capacity; Telus did not respond by press time.

From the source: According to an anonymous source quoted by The Globe and Mail, a lack of local support caused Telus to reconsider the project. Hundreds of people protested the data centre projects over the summer, and the sites are still awaiting municipal decisions, including rezoning and an upcoming city motion that could impose stricter requirements on data centre owners. The Globe’s source noted that the level of opposition in Vancouver would have made it challenging to proceed, but that Telus is still open to opportunities at these sites in the future.

The context: The Telus data centres were announced in May and were among the first to advance under the enabling large-scale sovereign AI data centres initiative, a federal program announced earlier this year designed to build domestic AI compute infrastructure and reduce reliance on foreign-owned systems. The proposed facilities included a 100,000-square-foot, repurposed facility in the Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, as well as a 400,000-square-foot development adjacent to Vancouver’s BC Place stadium.

Telus’ withdrawal from the project comes as the telecom giant is also facing mounting debt and is working to rejig its non-telecom sectors of the business. Its stock has fallen nearly 25 percent year-to-date.

Final thought: The recent federal budget pledged to enable Canadian AI companies to access 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute as foreign hyperscalers like Meta, Anthropic, and Microsoft buy up space in Canadian data centres. As building up sovereign compute capacity continues to be a government priority, a Westbank spokesperson said the firm has already chosen its new partners, who are Canadian and “will meet sovereignty requirements.”
